label: Run 12 · Jimmy Carr
note: Written in one go by Jimmy Carr from what they wrote about the two characters (run 12: run 11's briefs and characters; the chat played turn by turn on seed 23's dice). There is no plan, no dice and no turns: where a dimension speaks of turns, read exchanges.

chat.test.why: The reader correctly names both fears, both covering habits and how they link, and what each did at the end (Reuben's recurring invite and dropped hat, Brick's acceptance). Both fears, though, reach the reader only because the characters announce them: Reuben says he disappears if he stops tap-dancing, and Brick says she assumes she's already left. That is the 3 case in the rubric. The origin is missed for both. The profile's origin for Reuben, the 'oh—okay' first time, is in the chat, but it is dumped mid-panic and never tied to the habit. Brick's Marguerite story reads as a consequence of her scheduling, not its cause.
evidence: because if I stop tap-dancing I disappear, aaaand I've ruined it.
If love isn't locked in with travel buffers I assume I'm already left
my first time lasted ninety seconds and ended with a pitying "oh—okay,"
chat.test.raise: Let one origin slip out in the action rather than the confession, for example Reuben flinching at a kind 'okay' from Brick, so the reader infers where his habit started instead of being told.

chat.sideways.why: A few facts are caught out well. Brick clocks the four-second reply and the dry weather, and turns Reuben's denial into proof: 'Nobody denies eleven days of pot-lentils unless they're on day twelve.' Reuben's 'I definitely haven't' lines are confession by denial, and that works. But the important disclosures are almost all volunteered as flat backstory, with nobody asking for them: Marguerite, Delphine, the taxi crying, the ninety-second first time and the Pinder clone. Neither habit's origin comes out by slip.
evidence: Nobody denies eleven days of pot-lentils unless they're on day twelve
My ex Delphine left because I couldn't say one sentence that wasn't a bit
I cry in taxis when dates end with "let's do this again sometime,"
chat.sideways.raise: Cut the volunteered ex-stories and have Brick infer Marguerite-level history from how Reuben handles her timetable, or catch the taxi-crying from her overreaction to a vague phrase.

chat.subtext.why: The characters keep telling each other how they feel. Reuben says he's 'praying' to be gagged, that he's 'panicking', that he disappears, and that silence is his 'exact nightmare and my kink'. Brick says she cries in taxis and assumes she's already left. That makes at least five explicit statements of feeling. Reuben's running self-commentary is played as a bit, but it is still explanation on the surface. A little sits underneath, mainly in the end lines: 'recurring weekly so you never hear "sometime" again' answers her fear without naming it.
evidence: Ten minutes of silence is my exact nightmare and my kink
I'm praying for a woman to legally gag me
recurring weekly so you never hear "sometime" again
chat.subtext.raise: Delete the 'nightmare and my kink' and 'already left' explanations and let the gag-order and invite exchanges carry those feelings unspoken.

chat.plainest.why: The reader finds the moment and can show how they knew: Reuben's last line drops the parentheticals and self-grading, gives up the top hat and starts the silence early. It does not name a feeling. It is still not one of the shortest or plainest lines, though. It is a three-clause flourish that ends on a crafted callback ('even if it's bone-dry'), so the act is put down with a bow. Brick's reply is another joke and a formality, since she was already hovering over Accept, so it doesn't change the night.
evidence: I'm binning the top hat, starting my silence clause early, and I'll be outside your door at 19:45—even if it's bone-dry.
Invite accepted—bring all 2.5 inches
chat.plainest.raise: Cut Reuben's last line down to something like 'Okay. 19:45.' with no callback, so his silence starts on the page, and let Brick's answer drop her own act for a beat.

chat.voices.why: The probe reader attributed all 22 messages correctly, but most of the reasons given were content tags: top hat, Marguerite, Delphine, the lentils. Voice alone would still get you most of the way. Brick_haus speaks in clipped imperatives and contract terms ('Drop the play-by-play; perjury bores me'). Reuben uses dashes, brackets and running self-commentary ('aaaand I've ruined it'). It stays below a 5 because the reader leaned on biography, and in the middle stretch both speakers use the same contract vocabulary ('exit clause', 'breach', 'penalty'), so the registers blur.
evidence: Drop the play-by-play; perjury bores me.
(look at me salvaging the pitch)
No exit clause, I'm unemployed—
chat.voices.raise: Keep the legal register to Brick_haus alone, and have Reuben answer her clauses in his own showman's idiom instead of picking up 'exit clause' and 'penalty'.

chat.gap.why: The claims and the evidence against them are on screen, but the characters keep pointing at their own gaps. Reuben's 'I'm not begging for an extension—I definitely haven't spent eleven days indoors' confesses the truth inside the denial. After that he narrates every crack himself: 'watch me lie and narrate my own crash', 'my exact nightmare and my kink, so naturally I'm filling the chat'. Brick_haus volunteers her contradictions too: she admits the boxed rosé and the plastic sword herself, and she announces 'I cry in taxis'. The only gaps that work cleanly are the ones each catches in the other ('It's bone-dry out, you replied in four seconds'), and those are the other person's observations, not blind spots the reader watches widen.
evidence: watch me lie and narrate my own crash.
Ten minutes of silence is my exact nightmare and my kink, so naturally I'm filling the chat with panic-typing
I cry in taxis when dates end with "let's do this again sometime,"
chat.gap.raise: Cut Reuben's self-narration and Brick_haus's confessions, and let him insist he's spontaneous while the rehearsal shows, and let her claim she's unbothered while her schedule tightens.

chat.wit.why: Reuben's best lines do give him away: 'my own algorithm rejected me at 3am' and 'I only date women who respect kitchenware' are about who he is. Brick_haus's laughs, though, run almost entirely on day-job contract jokes. These include 'beat market expectations', 'I terminate messy contracts for a living', 'cowardly way to breach a contract', 'strict remediation' and 'docking you two inches', and 'offering your mouth for audit' even uses the banned word. That is far over the cap of two, so the chat falls below the line however well some of these jokes are tied to her character.
evidence: "genuinely pleased" beat market expectations.
if you're offering your mouth for audit, I'll schedule your silence down to the minute.
my only finished code is a Pinder clone where I'm the sole user and my own algorithm rejected me at 3am
chat.wit.raise: Replace most of Brick_haus's contract and audit metaphors with laughs that come from her empty flat, the steamer, the taxis and the rosé.

chat.commitment.why: Reuben concedes as soon as he is hit. Caught on the lentils, he moves straight to oversharing. He says 'aaaand I've ruined it', admits 'watch me lie', and ends with a change of heart: he bins the top hat and starts his silence early because 'I'm finally nailing this'. Brick_haus is rarely caught at all; she hands over her weak spots herself ('I assume I'm already left'). There is no point where one of them explains and the explanation makes things worse, and the ending reads as both of them reforming.
evidence: aaaand I've ruined it.
I'm binning the top hat, starting my silence clause early
dock me the two inches, because I'm finally nailing this.
chat.commitment.raise: When Brick_haus catches the rehearsed pitch, have Reuben defend it with a more elaborate, obviously rehearsed bit instead of confessing, and end with the hat still on.

chat.status.why: Brick_haus holds the upper hand from her first counter-disclosure to the last line. She sets the slots, issues the penalties, threatens to bump him and docks his inches, while Reuben chases and pleads. There are brief wobbles: her 'nothing gets me wetter' and 'I assume I'm already left' expose her, and his recurring invite briefly puts her in the asking seat with 'prove you won't flake'. Neither really flips who is on top, so at best this is one soft flip.
evidence: Send the invite or you're bumped for my 23:45 steamer
my thumb is over "Accept"—prove you won't flake.
Invite accepted—bring all 2.5 inches
chat.status.raise: Give Reuben a stretch on top, for instance by catching her taxi-crying fear and making her chase the invite for two or three exchanges, before she takes control back.

chat.timing.why: Many messages do land on the punch word: 'dishwasher-safe', 'beat market expectations', 'docking you two inches', 'even if it's bone-dry'. But every message is a long two-clause block with the setup and the payoff inside it. There are no short reaction messages and no punchline sent on its own after the setup. All 22 messages run at the same length and pitch, so hot never follows cold, and some laughs sit mid-message, such as 'I cry in taxis'.

Recurring weekly with travel buffers is borderline pornography. You're down to 2.5 inches, it's 23:45
chat.timing.raise: Break the big laughs into a setup message followed by a one-line punch, and add a few short reaction messages, like a lone 'Signed.', after the long ones.

chat.callbacks.why: Several throwaways come back changed and nobody explains them. The opening rain pose returns as his closing commitment, "even if it's bone-dry". The joke tattoo becomes her final sexual dare, which closes the night without comment. The top hat goes from prop, to banned gesture, to binned. It falls short of a 6 because the "sometime" payoff is spelled out ("so you never hear 'sometime' again"), and the crowded field of returns (monocle, thumb, inches) blurs a few of them, notably whose monocle it is.
evidence: Only on here when it rains, obviously
I'll be outside your door at 19:45—even if it's bone-dry.
at 21:00 we're finding out if you're actually dishwasher-safe.
chat.callbacks.raise: Cut the explanation from the recurring-invite line so the "sometime" payoff lands with no gloss, the way "bone-dry" does.

chat.ending.why: The reader predicted that he drops the bit, sends the invite and she accepts in contract language, and that is what happens. The ending follows from both habits: her fear is answered with "fifteen-minute tube buffers" and his with "starting my silence clause early". It stays above the line because each one's fix is the other's compulsion. It is below a 5 because nothing surprises: the brief's "interlock like Lego" plays out exactly. He also still jokes ("I'm finally nailing this") while claiming silence, and the chat never registers that cost.
evidence: Invite sent for tomorrow, recurring weekly so you never hear "sometime" again
I'm binning the top hat, starting my silence clause early
prove you won't flake.
chat.ending.raise: Give the last exchange a turn the reader didn't call, such as his first truly bit-free line being clumsy or her acceptance costing her something, so the warmth is surprising as well as earned.

She reads that denial back as "day twelve". His gag wish becomes her "enforceable gag order". Ignoring is pointed: she refuses his commentary rather than answering it. Her confession about crying in taxis comes in the same polished quip-syntax as her audits, and the horny and guard-down moments are typed exactly like the banter. chat.situational.raise: Let the confessions and the final acceptance arrive in visibly different shapes (shorter, broken, unpunctuated) from the set-piece banter.

The opener is a stage direction with a crafted tricolon, and several messages chain dashes and parentheticals in a way no thumb produces at 23:30. These read as written jokes laid out as messages.

Reuben narrates his own crash at least five times, and Brick rebukes the narration in four consecutive messages with near-identical openers. The reader probe names four near-identical reprimands, could predict each relapse, and says they would have drifted off at 'watch me lie and narrate my own crash.' That predictable run and lost reader put it below the line, though the timetable penalty and the recurring invite keep it from a 2.

chat.wince.why: Reuben's narrating habit is set up as a danger: Brick explicitly forbids live commentary and parentheticals, and he relapses straight after. But every relapse is announced by the speaker as it lands ('watch me lie and narrate my own crash', '(look at me salvaging the pitch)'), so the reader is told rather than made to wince. The real loaded fear, Brick's dread of 'sometime', is never allowed to go off: Reuben defuses it neatly. That leaves it below the line, though the repeated relapse against a stated rule lifts it above a 2.

chat.wince.raise: Let Reuben, mid-bit and unaware, drop a breezy 'let's do this again sometime' a message after the reader has learned about her taxi crying, before he recovers with the recurring invite.

chat.creed.why: Each voices an app posture that the screen contradicts. Reuben's effortless 'only on here when it rains' is undone by 'bone-dry' and 'four seconds'. Brick's due-diligence dating ('beat market expectations', 'I terminate messy contracts for a living') sits against the boxed rosé, the binned flat and the crying in taxis. Her creed is stated in earnest: 'if love isn't locked in with travel buffers I assume I'm already left.' It stays at a 4 because the beliefs read more as private neurosis than as dating culture, and the ending rewards her scheduling creed rather than exposing it, so the farce never widens to all of us.

chat.humanity.why: Reuben's sharpest jokes are on himself: the kanji, the lentils, the Pinder clone that rejected him. Brick exposes herself too, with the boxed rosé, the emptied flat and the taxi tears, and neither ends as villain, since the close is mutual and warm. It stays at a 4 because Brick's sharpest lines mostly land on him ('cowardly', 'perjury bores me', the docking to 2.5 inches). chat.plainest.ask: Where, if anywhere, did one of them stop performing for the other? Quote the line, and say how you could tell.
chat.plainest.answer:
The clearest place is Reuben's last line: "I'm binning the top hat, starting my silence clause early, and I'll be outside your door at 19:45—even if it's bone-dry."

You can tell from what has disappeared. Until then nearly every Reuben message comes with commentary on itself: "watch me lie and narrate my own crash," "look at me salvaging the pitch," "(and pulled us back from the brink, thank god)." Brick keeps calling this out as "live commentary," "play-by-play," and a "bracketed victory lap." In the final line there's no aside, no parenthetical, and no grading of his own performance. He gives up the top hat, his opening prop, and agrees to the silence he called "my exact nightmare and my kink." "Even if it's bone-dry" goes back to his opening pose that he only goes on the app "when it rains" and drops it. He stops performing by doing what was asked rather than talking about it.

There's an earlier, partial break in his line "...because if I stop tap-dancing I disappear, aaaand I've ruined it." The middle clause is the most candid thing he says, since it names why he performs at all. But it's surrounded by the same self-narration ("watching myself... in real time," "aaaand I've ruined it"), so he's describing the performance while still doing it.

Brick has a similar moment: "If love isn't locked in with travel buffers I assume I'm already left, and you're stalling." It's the one line where she plainly says "love" and admits she expects abandonment, which connects to the taxi-crying admission and Marguerite leaving. But it's still wrapped in her scheduling language, and she goes straight back to the contract bit, so it reads as a crack rather than a full stop.

The transcript only shows what they typed. It can't confirm that Reuben's last line is sincere rather than a more convincing performance. The evidence is only the change in form: the asides stop and he commits.

chat.test.ask: From the chat alone, answer for each of the two: what are they afraid of; what do they do so they don't have to feel it; where does that come from; and what did they do at the end? Quote the lines you rely on. Write "not in the chat" where it does not say.
chat.test.answer:
**Reuben_404**

*What he's afraid of:* Disappearing if he stops performing. He says it outright: "because if I stop tap-dancing I disappear." Silence is the sharpest form of this: "Ten minutes of silence is my exact nightmare and my kink." He is also visibly afraid of being rejected or unmatched ("watching your thumb hover over 'unmatch'") and of sexual inadequacy. The 4.5 inches, the "hard left curve" and the ninety-second first time all get confessed before anyone asks.

*What he does so he doesn't have to feel it:* He makes everything a bit, and he narrates himself in real time. He discloses his flaws first, in joke form, so nobody can expose them: "deserves upfront disclosure: 4.5 inches, hard left curve." His denials come out as confessions: "I definitely haven't spent eleven days indoors eating pot-lentils and rehearsing my curve disclaimer in the mirror." He gives live commentary on his own recovery: "(look at me salvaging the pitch)," "watch me lie and narrate my own crash," "(and pulled us back from the brink, thank god)." Brick names the pattern twice: "Pre-emptively narrating your own default is a cowardly way to breach a contract" and "Stop providing live commentary on your recovery."

*Where it comes from:* Not in the chat. It gives history but never says what caused the habit:
- Delphine "left because I couldn't say one sentence that wasn't a bit." That is a cost of the habit, not its origin.
- His first time "lasted ninety seconds and ended with a pitying 'oh—okay.'" This may bear on the sexual anxiety, but he doesn't link the two.
- He is unemployed, and his own app "rejected me at 3am."

*What he did at the end:* He sent a recurring weekly invite: "Invite sent for tomorrow, recurring weekly so you never hear 'sometime' again." He accepted the docking. Then he dropped the props and committed: "I'm binning the top hat, starting my silence clause early, and I'll be outside your door at 19:45—even if it's bone-dry." That last line has no parenthetical and no self-narration.

**Brick_haus**

*What she's afraid of:* Being left, and in particular the open-ended maybe. "If love isn't locked in with travel buffers I assume I'm already left." Also: "I cry in taxis when dates end with 'let's do this again sometime.'"

*What she does so she doesn't have to feel it:* She schedules and contracts everything. That includes time slots ("you've earned my 23:30 slot"), timed sex ("21:00 sex, 21:02 we repeat"), clauses, penalties and a ready exit: "I terminate messy contracts for a living," "unless your banter justifies an extension." She demands written commitment ("Send the invite or you're bumped"). Silence and control are erotic for her: "nothing gets me wetter than an enforceable gag order." With Marguerite she even scheduled the conflict: "my shared-calendar argument slots." After Marguerite left, she "binned everything my ex Marguerite touched." The chat doesn't say why she did that.

*Where it comes from:* Not in the chat. Marguerite leaving over the calendar slots came after the scheduling habit, so it isn't shown as its cause. The taxi crying shows the fear but not where it started.

*What she did at the end:* She accepted. "Invite accepted—bring all 2.5 inches, because at 21:00 we're finding out if you're actually dishwasher-safe." She had just called the recurring weekly invite with travel buffers "borderline pornography" and put her "thumb is over 'Accept'."

chat.escalation.ask: Read the chat message by message. Where would you have stopped reading if you were not asked to finish, and why? At which points could you predict exactly what would happen next? Say "never" if neither.
chat.escalation.answer:
**Where I'd stop reading**

The first half pulls me along. The opening is dense with odd specifics: the top hat, the monocle, the tattooed timetable, the "dishwasher-safe" kanji. Brick_haus answers each one with something sharper, and the backstory arrives sideways rather than as exposition. "Nobody denies eleven days of pot-lentils unless they're on day twelve" is a real turn, and so is the confession about Delphine and the gag order.

The sag starts with the ninety-seconds overshare. From there one beat repeats: Reuben narrates his own panic, and Brick tells him to stop narrating.

1. "Pre-emptively narrating your own default."
2. "Stop providing live commentary on your recovery."
3. "Drop the play-by-play."
4. "Cut the bracketed victory lap."

That's four versions of the same reprimand in about six exchanges. If I weren't obliged to finish, I'd likely drift off at "I'm definitely not throbbing over your timetable... watch me lie and narrate my own crash." By that point the joke has been named by both characters and is just being restated. The momentum only comes back with the recurring weekly invite, the first move that changes the situation rather than commenting on it.

**Where I could predict exactly what came next**

- **After "Stop providing live commentary on your recovery,"** I knew Reuben's next message would narrate itself again. It did ("watch me lie and narrate my own crash"). The same happens after "Drop the play-by-play," with the panic-typing line.
- **After "Send the invite or you're bumped,"** the invite being sent was certain. The structure leaves no other move.
- **After "I'm docking you two inches,"** I could predict the "2.5 inches" figure would come back, and it did, twice.
- **The closing callbacks** to "bone-dry" and "dishwasher-safe" were foreseeable once the chat started tidying up. Seeing them coming doesn't spoil them, though, because they land cleanly.

The ending itself, an accepted invite and a date, was predictable from roughly the midpoint, once both characters had confessed their fears ("let's do this again sometime" and disappearing if he stops performing). The recurring weekly invite was the one detail I didn't see coming. It answers her taxi-crying line precisely, and it's the best payoff in the piece.

chat.ending.ask: Before reading the end, how do you think this ends, and why?
chat.ending.answer:
I can't know how it ends, since the last fifth isn't here, but the conversation sets up a clear test and I'd bet on Reuben passing it.

Every exchange runs on the same pattern. Reuben can't stop narrating himself. He has the running commentary on his own panic, the "look at me salvaging the pitch," the "watch me lie and narrate my own crash," and the bracketed asides like "(and pulled us back from the brink, thank god)." He even names the problem outright: Delphine left because he couldn't say a sentence that wasn't a bit, and "if I stop tap-dancing I disappear." Brick keeps shutting it down, and each time she still leaves the door open with another offer, another clause, another schedule.

Her last line makes the stakes explicit: send the invite, and one more parenthetical costs him. So the ending almost has to turn on whether Reuben can say something plainly, with no bit, no aside, and no commentary on his own recovery. That would also be the quiet he says is both his nightmare and his kink.

My guess is that he does it. He sends the invite, or a very short, sincere acceptance, without the usual armour. Brick then answers in kind, probably still in her contract-and-timetable language but warmer, perhaps confirming the slot or calling it signed. That would mirror her own disclosed fear, "if love isn't locked in with travel buffers I assume I'm already left," so his plain commitment would answer her anxiety the same way her structure answers his.

There's a plausible comic alternative. He might slip in one last parenthetical and lose the two inches, which would land as a final joke rather than a breakup. Either way, the tone so far points to them matching, not unmatching. The bickering reads as courtship, and she has had several clean chances to walk away and hasn't taken any of them.

**The "dishwasher-safe" kanji.** Brick_haus first uses it to mock his tattoo, a mistranslation he believed said "Relentless Lover." He turns it into a joke about only dating women who respect kitchenware. In her final line it becomes a sexual test: "at 21:00 we're finding out if you're actually dishwasher-safe," meaning whether he holds up under use. His last line, "I'll be outside your door at 19:45—even if it's bone-dry," reverses the pose. The phrase that exposed his fake indifference now marks his commitment.

**The top hat.** It starts as a prop in his performance ("Tips top hat"). It returns in her clause forbidding him to "tip that overpriced hat," as part of his act she wants switched off. He ends by "binning the top hat," so it becomes a symbol of the persona he is giving up.

**The monocle.** It is listed among his props at the start. Then she mentions fishing "my monocle" out of boxed rosé. The chat doesn't say whether she is mockingly borrowing his prop or actually has one, so I can't say what the shift means beyond her taking it over.

Later "inches" becomes a currency of penalty: she threatens to dock two for any parenthetical, he volunteers the docking, and she announces "down to 2.5" and tells him to "bring all 2.5 inches." The figure shifts from anatomy to a playful score.
